title: Limits & Limit Laws
summary: A limit describes the value a function approaches as $x$ nears a point, even where the function is undefined. Limits can be read from tables and graphs, and computed with the limit laws — sums, products, quotients, and direct substitution for continuous pieces.

limit.plain: The value a function heads toward as the input approaches some number.
limit.in_class: Written $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$; the cornerstone of calculus.

one-sided limit.plain: The value approached from just the left or just the right of a point.
one-sided limit.in_class: $\lim_{x\to a^-}$ (left) and $\lim_{x\to a^+}$ (right); the two-sided limit exists only if they agree.

limit laws.plain: Rules that let you split a limit across sums, products, and quotients.
limit laws.in_class: e.g. $\lim(f+g)=\lim f+\lim g$; they reduce hard limits to simple pieces.

direct substitution.plain: Plugging the number straight into the function to get the limit.
direct substitution.in_class: Works whenever the function is continuous there: $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a)$.

indeterminate form.plain: An expression like $0/0$ that doesn't settle the limit on its own.
indeterminate form.in_class: Signals you must simplify (factor, rationalize) before the limit appears.

does not exist.plain: When a function approaches no single value (e.g. left ≠ right).
does not exist.in_class: Abbreviated DNE; common at jumps and vertical asymptotes.

squeeze theorem.plain: If a function is trapped between two others with equal limits, it shares that limit.

continuous.plain: A function with no breaks — you can draw it without lifting your pen.
continuous.in_class: For continuous functions the limit equals the function value.

concept_sections.heading: What a limit is
concept_sections.explanation: A limit asks: as $x$ gets arbitrarily close to $a$, what value does $f(x)$ approach? It does not care what happens right at $a$ — only nearby. You can estimate a limit numerically from a table of $x$-values closing in on $a$, or read it off a graph.
math_steps: Track the outputs $f(x)$ — do they settle on one number $L$?

concept_sections.heading: One-sided limits
concept_sections.explanation: Approaching from the left ($x\to a^-$) and the right ($x\to a^+$) can give different answers. The two-sided limit exists only when both one-sided limits exist and are equal. At a jump, they disagree and the limit does not exist.
math_steps: If they match, that common value is $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$; if not, the limit DNE.

concept_sections.heading: The limit laws
concept_sections.explanation: When the pieces have limits, the limit of a sum, difference, product, or quotient is the sum, difference, product, or quotient of the limits (quotient only if the denominator's limit is nonzero). Constants pull out and powers/roots pass through.
math_steps: Break the function into simple parts.
Apply the matching law: $\lim(f\pm g)=\lim f\pm\lim g$, $\lim(fg)=\lim f\cdot\lim g$.
For a quotient, use $\lim(f/g)=\lim f/\lim g$ when $\lim g\neq0$.

concept_sections.heading: Direct substitution
concept_sections.explanation: For polynomials, and any function continuous at $a$, the limit is just $f(a)$ — plug in. Substitution is always the first thing to try; if it gives a real number, you're done.
math_steps: If you get a finite number, that's the limit.
If you get $0/0$, the form is indeterminate — simplify first.

concept_sections.heading: Indeterminate forms $0/0$
concept_sections.explanation: When substitution yields $0/0$, the limit still may exist — you just have to reveal it. Factor and cancel the common term, or rationalize a radical, then substitute again.
math_steps: Substitute; if you get $0/0$, do not stop.
Factor numerator and denominator and cancel the shared factor (or multiply by a conjugate).
Substitute into the simplified expression to read off the limit.

real_world_examples.title: A car's instantaneous speed
real_world_examples.scenario: The speedometer shows speed at an instant, not over an interval.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Average speed over a shrinking time interval approaches a limit — the instantaneous speed. That limiting process is exactly $\lim_{\Delta t\to0}\Delta x/\Delta t$.

real_world_examples.title: Zooming a digital image
real_world_examples.scenario: Zoom in on a smooth curve and it looks straight.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: As the viewing window shrinks toward a point, the curve approaches its tangent line — a geometric limit underlying the derivative.

real_world_examples.title: Dosage approaching a steady level
real_world_examples.scenario: Repeated medication doses build toward a stable concentration.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The blood concentration approaches a limiting value as the number of doses grows — a real-world limit of a sequence of values.
